justification_text:
The point estimates at each horizon – 124.66 in this case – represent the central value I forecasted based on the available data or trends up to this point. Essentially, it's my best guess based on historical patterns, current conditions, and whatever forecasting model I employed. The fact that the point estimate stays constant across the 1-day, 1-week, and 1-month horizons suggests that I assumed limited directional change in the underlying variable over time, at least on average, though there is increasing uncertainty as the forecast moves further into the future.

The widths of the confidence intervals reflect the amount of uncertainty in the prediction at each time horizon. Close to the present, uncertainty tends to be lower because the system is less likely to experience dramatic changes overnight. However, as the time horizon lengthens, more variables come into play – emerging trends, external shocks, or compounding errors in the model – which cause the confidence intervals to widen. For instance, the 90% confidence interval for the 1-month horizon stretches notably wider than the 1-day or 1-week ranges, illustrating the natural growth of uncertainty over time due to the accumulation of unknown factors.

There are always risks or unexpected events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. External shocks like economic crises, political instability, sudden changes in policy, or unpredictable natural events could have a major impact, especially over the longer horizon, even if the confidence intervals were intended to account for "normal" uncertainties. Similarly, structural breaks in the data – like a significant shift in trends or relationships the model was based on – could render the forecast inaccurate. While I built the forecast and intervals to be robust under typical conditions, extraordinary or extreme events fall outside what the model assumes as plausible within 90% confidence.
